air_quality_exposure_screening.help_summary:
Air Quality / Urban Exposure

Land-use-regression-style screening grid, in the tradition Briggs et al. (1997) founded by showing that a handful of GIS-derivable proximity variables (road distance, source proximity) predict a large share of intra-urban NO2/PM variation without a dispersion model. Each cell's air_score sums road-proximity, emission-source-proximity and sensitive-receptor-density terms, then subtracts a green-buffer mitigation term (area share of GREEN_BUFFERS x BUFFER_WEIGHT) grounded in Nowak, Crane & Stevens' (2006) finding that urban tree canopy removes measurable particulate mass in open settings. That subtraction is not universal, though: Vos et al. (2013) found dense roadside planting in an enclosed street canyon can trap pollutants and raise local concentration by reducing ventilation - green buffers help most in open contexts, not narrow canyons.

ROAD_DISTANCE (default 300 m) and SOURCE_DISTANCE (default 600 m) are linear decay-to-zero radii, not measured plume extents - road distance in particular tracks the near-road influence zone widely used in traffic-related air pollution (TRAP) exposure studies. Sensitive-receptor density is capped at 4 receptors per cell (25 points each); source and sensitive layers are optional and read as 0 contribution when omitted.

How to read the results - air_score >= 75: within about 50 m of a major road or downwind of an industrial source, with no offsetting green buffer - the environmental-justice hotspots. - green_share is diagnostic, not just decorative: a high air_score despite a large green_share means the road/source pressure is strong enough to overwhelm the mitigation credit, or (per Vos et al., 2013) the planting sits in a canyon where it may not be helping at all. - Exposed sensitive receptors are only written for cells scoring >= 55 - schools, hospitals or housing that clear that bar are the intervention shortlist.

Using the results: overlay with the Urban Heat Comfort Risk grid to find cells that are both hot and polluted (double environmental burden), and cross-reference with Social Vulnerability Index to test whether pollution exposure and social vulnerability coincide in the same neighbourhoods. This is not an atmospheric dispersion model - it has no wind, stability class, or source-strength term. Use it for first-pass spatial screening and siting new green buffers in open areas; do not use it for regulatory compliance or health-risk quantification, which need modelled or monitored concentrations.

parameters.name: EMISSION_SOURCES
parameters.label: Industrial / emission sources (optional point or polygon)

apply_resilience_symbology.help_summary:
Apply Resilience Symbology

Applies a consistent, colourblind-conscious PlanX colour preset to a scored or classified resilience layer. Every tool in this suite that produces a 0-100 score or a fixed class set (Covered/Watch/Underserved/ Critical/Unreachable; Improved/Stable/Worsened; Monitor/Medium/High/ Immediate) uses the same breakpoints and labels throughout - this tool exists to share ONE colour vocabulary across the whole plugin, so "red means Very High" only needs learning once.

Use it after generating risk grids, accessibility outputs, scenario comparison layers, or adaptation priority synthesis outputs. The algorithm styles the selected layer in-place (a side effect, not a new output layer) and can optionally save a QML style file for reuse.

Using the results: the four presets only work if the target field's values or labels match exactly what each preset expects (0-100 numeric for the risk-score preset, the exact string labels for the others) - a field using different terminology or a different numeric range needs reconciling with this suite's naming convention first.

bivariate_choropleth_symbology.help_summary:
Bivariate Choropleth Symbology

Classifies every feature into Low / Mid / High on two scored axes (e.g., risk and vulnerability) using tertile breaks, then assigns the 9-category Stevens-style bivariate palette - a cartographic convention popularised specifically because a single-variable map cannot answer "where are BOTH high at once," which is exactly the equity-and-exposure double-burden question this shows at a glance.

Output layer adds bv_class (e.g. R-H_V-M), bv_risk_bin and bv_vuln_bin fields and comes with a categorised renderer already applied.

Tertile breaks are computed from the SUPPLIED layer's own value range - the same extent-relative caveat as Social Vulnerability Index's normalisation: re-running on a different extent moves the Low/Mid/High boundaries even for identical values. A 3x3 matrix is a deliberate resolution limit; finer binning becomes hard to decode visually.

Reads beautifully alongside a 3×3 legend grid placed in the print layout (no built-in legend item is generated — place it manually as a cartographic element).

Using the results: check Multi-Hazard Correlation Matrix first if the two input fields might be strongly correlated - a bivariate map of two nearly-identical fields wastes the second colour dimension on redundant information.

parameters.name: INPUT
parameters.label: Polygon layer with two score fields

climate_adaptation_priority_synthesis.help_summary:
Climate Adaptation Priority Synthesis

Linear weighted-sum multi-criteria composite - the simplest, most transparent form of MCDA, following the same additive aggregation logic as the ISO 14044 lifecycle-impact convention. Combines up to eight 0-100 hazard fields (heat, flood, social, air, access, drought, wildfire/WUI, coastal/SLR) with auditable weights chosen so no single hazard dominates by construction - the weights are the explicit, auditable policy choice.

Linear weighted-sum means full compensability: a very low flood score can offset a very high heat score. Missing fields are excluded and their weight redistributed across present fields - a unit with only 2 of 8 fields still gets a score, but check the missing field before treating it as equally reliable to a fully-populated unit. All inputs must already be on a common 0-100 scale; this tool performs no normalisation.

How to read the results - adapt_score: the composite ranking number, 0-100. - adapt_class: Immediate (>=75) / High (55-74) / Medium (35-54) / Monitor (<35). - drivers: which hazard(s) actually drove the score - "flood:92.1, heat:45.0" means a flood priority, not a heat one; use this to assign hazard-specific interventions rather than generic ones. - missing: fields absent or zero-weighted - a reliability check, not a score component.

Using the results: this algorithm does not spatially join layers by itself - prepare one polygon layer via Join Hazard Scores to Planning Units first. Feed adapt_score into Equity-Adjusted Priority to re-rank by vulnerability, or into Risk-Recovery Priority Matrix with a recovery score to find high-hazard + low-recovery gaps. Where the breakdown of which hazard drives the score matters more than the single number, use Multi-Hazard Composite Index instead - it keeps the diagnostic breakdown visible rather than collapsing it away.

climate_projection_overlay.help_summary:
Climate Projection Overlay

Applies a single literature-derived amplification factor to today's hazard/composite score, trading physical downscaling fidelity for accessibility - no CMIP/regional-climate-model raster stack required. Built-in factors are drawn from IPCC AR6 WG1 regional fact sheets, which project heatwave frequency increases of roughly 1.3-1.6x per degree of warming and flood magnitude increases of roughly 1.1-1.5x.

Scenarios:

  • Stable (today) - factor 1.00
  • Mild (+1.5C, ~2050) - factor 1.15
  • Moderate (+2C, ~2070) - factor 1.30
  • High (+3C, ~2100) - factor 1.60
  • Custom - use the explicit factor parameter

A single scalar cannot represent how climate change reshapes the SPATIAL PATTERN of a hazard, only its overall magnitude - today's geographic distribution of exposure is assumed to persist unchanged, which is frequently false (e.g. sea-level rise shifts WHERE flooding occurs, not just how much). The clamp at 100 means a unit already near the ceiling shows little visible delta even under an aggressive scenario.

How to read the results: cp_delta_class = Major increase (>25 points) flags units that cross a risk-class threshold under the scenario (e.g. Moderate 45 -> High 72) - the units where climate change qualitatively changes the risk profile, not just the number.

Using the results: run all four built-in scenarios and compare the Major-increase counts to show the non-linear escalation of risk. For hazard-specific factors (heat 1.3, flood 1.5, etc.) run the algorithm once per hazard with a Custom factor - the built-in factors are generic cross-hazard averages, not hazard- or location-specific projections. Where decision stakes justify it, commission real downscaled climate projections instead of relying on this generic scalar.

parameters.name: CUSTOM_FACTOR
parameters.label: Custom amplification factor (used only if scenario = Custom)

coastal_slr_exposure.group: 3 - Flood & Coastal: Pluvial and SLR Susceptibility
coastal_slr_exposure.help_summary:
Coastal / Sea-Level-Rise (SLR) Exposure Screening

Evaluates coastal inundation and sea-level-rise (SLR) plus storm-surge exposure using a hydrologically connected bathtub flood-fill model (Poulter & Halpin, 2008; Gesch, 2009; Nicholls & Cazenave, 2010). Unlike a naive elevation threshold that falsely flags disconnected inland topographic pits below the target water level, this algorithm runs a breadth-first search (BFS) from coastline-adjacent submerged cells across either 8-connected or 4-connected grid neighbours so only hydrologically connected cells (connected = 1) receive full inundation scoring.

For each grid cell, the 0-100 slr_score combines connected inundation depth (inund_m) or low freeboard margin (freeboard_m within 2.0 m above the design water level), coastal proximity within NEAR_SHORE_BUFFER_M, and exposed building/road asset density. Isolated low-lying inland depressions below the design water level are tagged with connected = 0 and sink_depth > 0 for diagnostic inspection.

How to read the results: cells scoring slr_score >= 55 or hydrologically connected submerged cells (connected = 1) are written to the priority coastal zone output, and structures located inside impacted cells are exported as point features to the exposed coastal structures layer.

parameters.name: COASTLINE
parameters.label: Coastline / shoreline or marine water body (line or polygon)

parameters.name: BUILDINGS
parameters.label: Buildings / coastal structures (optional polygon or point)

parameters.name: WATER_LEVEL_M
parameters.label: Custom water level above datum (m, used when Custom selected)

parameters.name: NEAR_SHORE_BUFFER_M
parameters.label: Coastal wave / surge proximity buffer (map units)

cost_benefit_analyzer.help_summary:
Cost-Benefit Analyzer

Ranks planning units by cost-effectiveness using a transparent two-input model - the standard, textbook first-pass prioritisation method in public-sector economic appraisal (Boardman et al., 2018), simpler and faster than a full NPV analysis (see the sibling Lifecycle Cost Calculator for that) but able to rank hundreds of candidates in one pass:

 cost = unit_cost × area benefit = score × reduction_factor × population_weight ratio = benefit / cost

Either a single default unit cost / reduction factor or per-feature fields can be supplied. Population weighting is optional. The reduction factor (default 0.7) is a planning-level estimate of how much risk the intervention removes, not an engineering-validated figure for any specific design. The output layer also includes a 1-N priority rank so you can drive a print layout straight from it.

The processing log prints the cumulative-budget curve — useful for finding the "to capture 80 % of benefit you need to fund 25 % of units" breakpoint.

Using the results: the B/C ratio says nothing about absolute budget - pair rank with the absolute cb_cost/cb_benefit values, not the ratio alone. Feed cb_priority_rank == 1 features into Pareto-Optimal Selector to find the full cost-benefit frontier; ratio-ranking and Pareto selection can disagree when absolute costs vary widely across candidates.

parameters.name: UNIT_COST
parameters.label: Default unit cost (currency / m² for polygons; / feature for points)

critical_infrastructure_exposure.help_summary:
Critical Infrastructure Exposure

Crosses a hazard score layer with a critical-facility layer (schools, hospitals, fire stations, water/power assets) combining hazard risk assessment with infrastructure-interdependency theory (Rinaldi, Peerenboom & Kelly, 2001): a facility is critical not only for the function it delivers directly, but because failures elsewhere (power, water, roads) can knock it out too. The multiplicative hazard x criticality form follows the standard R = H x V x E risk equation (UNDRR, 2019).

combined = (hazard / 100) × (criticality_norm) × 100 where criticality_norm linearly maps the user's raw criticality field to 0-100 using its own min and max - usable with any scale (1-5, 1-100, replacement value, population served) without prior knowledge of the bounds, but only meaningful relative to the other facilities in this run. Hazard is sampled by polygon CONTAINMENT of the facility centroid, not intersection - a facility spanning two hazard zones is scored entirely by whichever zone contains its centre.

If no criticality field is given, every facility uses the default criticality so the output is essentially the hazard score sampled at each facility.

Using the results: feed the top-N facilities into Cost-Benefit Analyzer to rank retrofit options. This scores single-facility, single-snapshot exposure only - it has no representation of cascading, network-level interdependency failures (Buldyrev et al., 2010); a facility scoring Low here could still be knocked out by a dependency this tool cannot see. It is not a substitute for a genuine infrastructure-interdependency simulation study (Ouyang, 2014 reviews those methods) where cascading failure is the actual concern.

parameters.name: CRITICALITY_DEFAULT
parameters.label: Default criticality if no field given

emergency_accessibility_shelter_coverage.help_summary:
Emergency Accessibility and Shelter Coverage

Euclidean nearest-shelter screening in the accessibility tradition Hansen (1959) founded (access as a function of distance to opportunity) and Radke & Mu (2000) operationalised for service planning as the two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method, later refined by Luo & Wang (2003) for healthcare access. This tool implements the simplest member of that family: a single-step distance-decay score to the nearest shelter, without 2SFCA's catchment-overlap correction or supply/demand ratio (both need a shelter capacity field, which this tool does not take by design).

access_score ramps linearly from 0 at SERVICE_DISTANCE to 100 at CRITICAL_DISTANCE, plus an additive barrier-overlap penalty (BARRIER_WEIGHT x share of the cell covered by BARRIERS) standing in for the detour a real barrier (river, highway without a crossing) would force - it can only push the score toward worse, it never recomputes an actual reroute. Only the nearest shelter counts; the model has no notion of that shelter's remaining capacity.

How to read the results - access_class Critical: >75% of the way from service to critical distance - no nearby shelter at all. - Underserved: 55-74%. Watch: 35-54%, in reach but not comfortable. Covered: <35%. - barrier_pct is diagnostic: a cell can have a short dist_shelter but still score poorly if it sits mostly behind a barrier polygon.

Using the results: cross-reference underserved assets with Social Vulnerability Index to find vulnerable populations with poor shelter access. Use this for a first-pass screening pass with no road data on hand. Switch to Network Emergency Accessibility anywhere real routing barriers matter (rivers, highways, one-way systems), and to Evacuation Time Simulation or Optimal Shelter Siting for any decision that needs to account for shelter capacity - this tool deliberately does not.

parameters.name: SHELTERS
parameters.label: Shelters / safe assembly areas (point or polygon)

equity_adjusted_priority.help_summary:
Equity-Adjusted Adaptation Priority

Re-ranks adaptation priority by multiplying a hazard/composite score (0-100) with an equity factor derived from the Social Vulnerability Index (0-100), following the distributive-justice framework for climate adaptation (Shi et al., 2016): resources should be allocated proportional to both physical exposure AND social vulnerability, since treating hazard score alone as the ranking criterion implicitly assumes every unit has equal capacity to respond.

Equity factor: 1 + w * (SVI / 100)

  • w = 0 -> result equals the raw hazard score (no adjustment, the neutral default).
  • w = 1 -> a fully vulnerable unit doubles in priority.
  • w = 0.5 (default) -> SVI=100 gets a 50% boost.

The adjustment is multiplicative, not additive: a unit with a very low hazard score gains little absolute priority even at high SVI, since there's little to amplify - this tool re-ranks AMONG already-hazardous units by vulnerability, it does not manufacture priority from vulnerability alone. SVI must already be joined onto the same layer; this tool computes no vulnerability score of its own.

How to read the results: units where eq_adjusted_score exceeds eq_hazard by more than 10 points are the equity finding - physically moderate hazard but high social vulnerability pushed them up the list.

Using the results: use w=0.5 for balanced prioritisation, w=1.0 for a strongly equity-first ranking - but treat the weight choice itself as a policy decision for affected communities to weigh in on, not a purely technical one. Adjusted score is normalized back to 0-100 so it remains comparable across runs and joinable with other resilience layers.

evacuation_shelter_arrival_summary.help_summary:
Evacuation Shelter Arrival Summary

Aggregates assigned evacuation origins into per-shelter arrival curves - cumulative-arrival-curve analysis is a standard tool in emergency operations planning (FEMA, 2019; NIST, 2015). Use evac_timestep from queue-mode evacuation, or bin evac_min when timestep is unavailable. P50/P95 time-to-capacity operationalise "shelter service speed" - a shelter reaching 90% capacity in the first 10 minutes has a compressed arrival profile (nearby, unimpeded catchment); one reaching only 30% after 40 minutes has a distant catchment, congested access routes, or both.

Outputs a table with arrivals and cumulative population per shelter/step, plus an optional HTML summary with a stacked-bar timeline per shelter.

This tool is a pure post-processor: it adds no new routing or capacity logic, so every assumption of the parent Evacuation Time Simulation (perfect compliance, no shadow evacuation, hard capacity caps) carries through unchanged. TIMESTEP_MINUTES here should match the upstream simulation's own timestep for the P50/P95 figures to correspond to real decision points.

Using the results: a shelter whose final cumulative_pct falls short of 100% signals unassigned or queue-stalled origins in the PARENT simulation - trace back to its qa_flag field rather than debugging here. Bimodal arrival curves suggest two distinct catchment sub-populations; consider splitting the distant one to a closer shelter. Running this on an instant-assignment (TIMESTEP_MINUTES=0) simulation collapses the arrival profile to a simple travel-time histogram, losing the congestion story this tool is built to surface.

parameters.name: MINUTES_FIELD
parameters.label: Total evacuation minutes field (fallback, e.g. evac_min)

evacuation_time_simulation.help_summary:
Evacuation Time Simulation

Greedy capacity-constrained shelter assignment with optional timestep queueing, in the macroscopic-flow tradition Daganzo's (1994) Cell Transmission Model established: discretise time into steps and cap how much flow crosses a link per step, without simulating individual vehicles. Yperman's (2007) Link Transmission Model refined that for large networks; TIMESTEP_MINUTES here is a simplified, planning-scale instance of the same discretised-flow-with-capacity-cap logic. Shelter assignment itself is a greedy nearest-capacity heuristic in the Church & ReVelle (1974) facility-location tradition.

Assignment is order-dependent: ASSIGN_ORDER (farthest-first vs largest-population-first) changes which shelters fill and which origins go unassigned, because greedy locks in early decisions later origins must live with. Road capacity is a fixed persons/hour ceiling with no speed-density degradation as flow approaches it - real traffic flow slows non-linearly near jam density, which this hard cap does not represent. Timestep minutes = 0 means instant greedy assignment, no queueing.

How to read the results - qa_flag = no_capacity: population that could not be assigned - it does not vanish, it needs more shelter capacity or more sites (feed into Optimal Shelter Siting). - congestion_pct > 100 on an edge: assigned load exceeds its hourly capacity - a bottleneck. - P95 evacuation time (in the log): the time by which 95% of assigned population has reached a shelter; compare instant vs timestep-queue mode to see the congestion delay.

Using the results: feed congested edges into Cost-Benefit Analyzer to rank road-widening interventions. This model assumes perfect compliance - no shadow evacuation (people leaving who weren't told to) or evacuation refusal, both well-documented real behaviours (Murray-Tuite & Wolshon, 2013). Use it for macro-scale screening and assignment-order sensitivity, not for micro-level traffic-engineering decisions (signal timing, lane geometry) - that needs a true microsimulation.

parameters.name: ROAD_DIRECTION_FIELD
parameters.label: Road direction field (optional: both / ft / bt)

green_infrastructure_drought_stress.group: 7 - Drought & Wildfire: Green and WUI Stress
green_infrastructure_drought_stress.help_summary:
Drought and Green Infrastructure Stress

Ranks green-infrastructure patches by drought/thermal stress sensitivity, combining island-biogeography edge effects (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967 - smaller patches have a higher edge-to-core ratio, so more of their area is exposed to the surrounding matrix's microclimate) with McDonald et al.'s (2008) finding that impervious cover within roughly 100-200 m of a green patch measurably raises its local temperature and moisture stress. The 0-100 stress_score is a weighted mean of impervious context (share of impervious surface in a buffer around the patch, radius = MAX_WATER_DISTANCE x 0.25), distance to the nearest water feature, a small-patch penalty (relative to the size range of the supplied layer), and a tree-density deficit (fewer TREES points nearby = higher stress) using the i-Tree Eco sampling convention (Nowak et al., 2008).

Patch-size scoring is relative to this run's input set - adding one very large park re-ranks every other patch's size component even though nothing about them changed physically. Without a TREES layer, every patch's tree-density term reads worst-case (100) unless TREE_WEIGHT is zeroed. Patches scoring >= 55 are written to a second, priority-intervention output.

How to read the results - stress_score >= 75: small, isolated patches surrounded by impervious surface, far from water, with sparse trees - acute drought vulnerability. - tree_count = 0 is a planting opportunity flag, not necessarily a crisis - it means no tree points were supplied for that patch, check the TREES input coverage before acting on it. - size_score is only meaningful relative to the other patches in the same run; it is not an absolute area threshold.

Using the results: feed high-priority patches into Cost-Benefit Analyzer to rank irrigation and tree-planting interventions by cost-effectiveness, and cross-reference with Population-Weighted Exposure (using nearby population polygons) to quantify how many people depend on each stressed green space. This is an ecological screening index from geometry and land-cover context alone - it has no soil-moisture data and no plant physiology model. Do not use it to diagnose actual plant water stress or to schedule irrigation; use remote-sensing NDVI/NDWI or soil-moisture sensors for that.

parameters.name: WATER
parameters.label: Water / blue infrastructure (optional line or polygon)

hazard_frequency_aggregation.help_summary:
Multi-Period Hazard Frequency Aggregation

Collapse N temporal hazard snapshots (e.g., the same flood model run for 2020 / 2030 / 2050, or seismic Monte Carlo across magnitudes) into ONE composite per planning unit, addressing the temporal-compounding problem in risk assessment (IPCC, 2012; Zscheischler et al., 2018): a unit scoring 80 in every period represents a fundamentally different risk than one scoring 95 once and 30 otherwise, even with an identical mean.

All source layers must share the same score field name. The threshold tau (default 50) is a single global cutoff applied identically to every period. Frequency-weighted mean penalises single-period spikes by design - a genuinely catastrophic one-off event scores lower on this composite than a chronically moderate hazard; use Max mode when worst-case, not average, preparedness is the question.

Output fields:

  • hf_frequency — count of source layers whose intersecting score exceeds the threshold at this unit.
  • hf_mean / hf_max / hf_min — statistics of the scores across the source layers.
  • hf_composite — Mean, Max, or Frequency-weighted mean depending on the chosen mode. Frequency-weighted mean = mean × (freq / N) so units that score high in BOTH many periods AND high intensity rise to the top.
  • hf_class — Very High / High / Moderate / Low based on the composite.

Using the results: hf_frequency = N (every period above threshold) flags persistent, chronic exposure needing structural adaptation, not just emergency response. Feed the output into Climate Projection Overlay for a second temporal-stress dimension, or Scenario Sensitivity Analysis to test whether rank is stable when threshold tau varies. Use this for the SAME hazard across different time periods or scenarios - for genuinely different hazards, use Multi-Hazard Composite Index instead.

parameters.name: SCORE_FIELD
parameters.label: Score field name (same on every source)

hotspot_analysis_getis_ord.help_summary:
Hot-Spot Cluster Analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*)

Tags each feature as a statistically significant hot spot (cluster of high values), cold spot (cluster of low values), or not significant, based on its neighbours' values - answering not just "is there clustering somewhere" but WHERE specifically. Gi* (as opposed to Gi) includes the feature itself in its own neighbourhood sum, which behaves better at dataset edges and is the standard variant in practice. Use on any 0-100 resilience score: composite, social vulnerability, recovery capacity, etc.

Outputs added to each feature:

  • gi_zscore - standardised statistic; |z| > 1.65 ~ 90% confidence.
  • gi_pvalue - two-sided p-value derived from z.
  • gi_p_fdr - Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted p-value (controls false discoveries across the n simultaneous local tests).
  • gi_class - Hot-99 / Hot-95 / Hot-90 / Not significant / Cold-90 / Cold-95 / Cold-99.
  • gi_class_fdr - same labels from the FDR-adjusted p-value; prefer this when reporting.

Spatial weights are either inverse distance (row-standardised) or a fixed-distance band (1 if within distance, else 0). Self is always included (Gi*, not Gi).

Gi* assumes the value field is at least approximately normally distributed - a handful of extreme outliers can distort results (try a log or rank transform for strongly skewed fields). The DISTANCE band and weight method materially change which features get flagged; running at 2-3 different bands to check stability is standard practice, not optional. gi_class will always flag more features than gi_class_fdr - report which one you mean.

Using the results: where outliers (a high value surrounded by low neighbours, or vice versa) are the object of interest rather than clusters, use LISA Local Moran's I instead - Gi* is built to find clusters, not outliers.

join_scores_to_planning_units.display_name: Join Hazard Scores to Planning Units
join_scores_to_planning_units.help_summary:
Join Hazard Scores to Planning Units

Attaches up to five 0-100 score fields onto planning-unit polygons by taking the MAXIMUM score among intersecting features per unit - a deliberately conservative, precautionary-principle choice: if any part of a unit is exposed to a high score, the whole unit inherits it. This avoids the dilution problem of areal-weighted averaging, where a small high-hazard sliver (a flood-prone stream corridor crossing a large tract) gets averaged away by the tract's mostly-low-hazard area - an instance of the wider Modifiable Areal Unit Problem.

The five source layers are joined independently with no cross-layer normalisation - they only stay comparable because every hazard tool in this suite outputs 0-100 by convention. A NULL joined field means "no intersecting feature," never "zero risk" - do not conflate the two in a downstream composite.

How to read the results - Each OUT field is the max score from its source layer; check for NULLs before running a composite, since a composite treating NULL as 0 silently understates risk instead of flagging missing data. - Cross-score consistency: sort by each joined field and compare top-10 lists - overlapping lists mean a concentrated multi-hazard problem, disjoint lists mean the hazards are spatially independent.

Using the results: this is the standard "collect and align" step - run Heat / Flood / Social / Air / Drought first, join here, then feed into Multi-Hazard Composite Index or Climate Adaptation Priority Synthesis. Where an areal-weighted average is more defensible than max-intersection (aggregating a fine grid onto large administrative units), pre-process with zonal statistics instead.

lifecycle_cost_calculator.help_summary:
Lifecycle Cost Calculator

Per unit, computes the discounted Net Present Value of an intervention over a configurable horizon (default 25 years, 4% discount rate) - the standard engineering-economics method for comparing long-term investment alternatives (Fuller & Petersen, 1996; ISO 15686-5:2017). Includes capex, annual opex, periodic maintenance and replacement events, annualised via the capital recovery factor so interventions with different lifespans can be compared fairly.

The discount rate and all recurring costs are treated as constant for the whole horizon - real public discount rates and maintenance costs can vary over time, which this model does not represent; treat outputs as expected-value planning estimates, not guaranteed budgets.

Outputs lc_capex_npv, lc_opex_npv, lc_maintenance_npv, lc_replacement_npv, lc_total_npv, lc_annualised (equivalent flat annual cost over the horizon).

If Area scaling is on and the input is polygon, all per-m² fields are multiplied by polygon area (no economies of scale represented); otherwise they are used literally per feature.

Using the results: lc_annualised is the most communicable number - "this costs X per year, flat, for 25 years." lc_maintenance_npv > lc_capex_npv flags a maintenance-heavy intervention (common in green infrastructure) that should be budgeted for accordingly. Use this for the rigorous total-cost-of-ownership comparison across a shortlist - for fast first-pass screening across many candidates, Cost-Benefit Analyzer's simpler ratio model is faster to populate.

parameters.name: MAINT_COST
parameters.label: Default maintenance event cost (used if no field)

parameters.name: REPL_COST
parameters.label: Default replacement cost (used if no field)

parameters.name: AREA_SCALE
parameters.label: Scale per-unit-area values by polygon area

lisa_local_moran.help_summary:
LISA Local Moran's I

Companion to the Hot-Spot Gi* module - Anselin's (1995) Local Indicators of Spatial Association decompose the global Moran's I into per-feature contributions, and crucially classify each feature by comparing its own value against its neighbourhood's spatial lag - which is what lets LISA detect OUTLIERS as well as clusters, a capability Gi* (built purely to find clusters) structurally lacks. For each feature:

  • HH — high value in a high-value neighbourhood (cluster).
  • LL — low value in a low-value neighbourhood (cluster).
  • HL — high value surrounded by low neighbours (outlier) - e.g. a well-resourced pocket in an under-served district.
  • LH — low value surrounded by high neighbours (outlier) - the equity gap Gi* cannot see.
  • Not significant at the 95 % level.

Significance uses the analytic randomization moments of Anselin (1995) — per-feature E[I] and Var[I] from the row-standardised weights and sample kurtosis. With very few features, these moment estimates become unstable, undermining the significance test that depends on them. Because n local tests run simultaneously, a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted p-value (lisa_p_fdr) and the corresponding conservative quadrant label (lisa_quad_fdr) are also written — prefer those when reporting results.

Using the results: feed HL and LH units into Equity-Adjusted Priority to see whether the equity adjustment changes their rank. Where only cluster strength matters and outliers are not of interest, Gi*'s continuous z-score is a more direct answer without LISA's added HL/LH classification overhead.

multi_hazard_composite_index.help_summary:
Multi-Hazard Composite Index

Combines N hazard score fields (0-100 each) into one composite, in the spirit of the IPCC AR5 "reasons for concern" framework that assesses multiple climate risks jointly rather than hazard-by-hazard - a place facing three moderate stresses can be more fragile than one facing a single severe stress. On top of the composite, this tool computes a Shannon (1948) entropy diversity index: 0 means one hazard explains everything (concentrated, one clear intervention target), 100 means all hazards contribute equally (diffuse, no single fix suffices) - exactly the axis a plain weighted-sum score discards, since two units can share an identical composite while having completely different risk profiles.

Diversity is computed on each hazard's relative weighted contribution, normalised by ln(N) where N is the number of fields supplied in THIS run - mh_diversity values are only directly comparable across units analysed with the same field count.

Outputs added to each feature:

  • mh_score - weighted mean of hazard scores (0-100).
  • mh_class - Very High / High / Moderate / Low.
  • mh_dominant - field name with the largest weighted contribution; the hazard to target first.
  • mh_diversity - 0 (single hazard dominant) to 100 (multi-stressed across all hazards).
  • mh_drivers - top 3 contributing field names (CSV).
  • mh_data_gap - number of hazard fields with null or non-numeric values; a nonzero value means the composite is based on incomplete data.

Weights: optional CSV string matching the order of selected fields. Empty -> equal weights. Negative -> clamped to 0.

Using the results: units combining high mh_score with high mh_diversity are the most complex cases - feed them into Scenario Sensitivity Analysis to test whether their rank is stable under weight uncertainty. Where a single simple composite is all that's needed for reporting, use the leaner Climate Adaptation Priority Synthesis instead.

multi_hazard_correlation_matrix.help_summary:
Multi-Hazard Correlation Matrix

Pairwise Pearson (linear) and Spearman (rank/monotonic, robust to outliers) correlations between N numeric score fields on the same layer - highly correlated fields (|r| > 0.80) contribute redundant spatial information to a composite index, inflating its sensitivity to shared measurement error (OECD, 2008 composite-indicator guidance). Output is a standalone HTML report with a colour-coded heatmap, top correlations table, and per-pair diagnostics.

Use case: spot redundancy in a composite ("seismic and flood already move together in this city") or surprise divergences ("heat is uncorrelated with everything else").

Also returns a long-format table (field_a / field_b / pearson_r / spearman_r / n_pairs) for further joining or styling. Missing values are excluded PAIRWISE, so n_pairs can differ across the table - always check it alongside the coefficient before trusting a strong correlation from very few valid pairs.

Using the results: run this before building any multi-hazard composite to inform weight choices and which fields to include - correlation measures association, not causation, and spatial data is never truly independent (spatial autocorrelation), so treat the strength labels as descriptive, not formal hypothesis tests.

parameters.name: INPUT
parameters.label: Layer with multiple numeric score fields

network_criticality.help_summary:
Network Criticality (edge betweenness proxy)

Betweenness centrality (Freeman, 1977) measures how much shortest-path traffic flows through an edge, summed over every origin-destination pair - exact computation (Brandes, 2001) is O(VE), too slow for interactive QGIS use on a real road network. This tool narrows the scope instead: the shortest path from each real ORIGIN to its single nearest real DESTINATION only, an origin-destination usage-count proxy that trades betweenness's generality for realism (an actual emergency-access flow pattern) and speed (O(origins x edges log vertices)). Closer in spirit to traffic-assignment-based criticality than to graph-theoretic betweenness proper.

usage_count is a raw frequency count, criticality_score = 100 x usage_count / max usage_count within this run - not comparable across runs with different origin/destination sets. Each origin routes to its single nearest destination only; if that shelter fills up, the "next nearest" reassignment this implies never actually happens here.

How to read the results - criticality_score is a busy-ness measure, not a removal-impact measure. A busy edge with parallel alternatives costs little to lose; a quiet edge can still be the ONLY connector for a small demand pocket - usage_count alone cannot tell these two cases apart. - criticality_score >= 90 marks the busiest few percent of edges under normal, all-shelters-available routing.

Using the results: pair with Evacuation Time Simulation's per-edge load output to check whether the busiest corridors also carry the highest congestion, and with Seismic Cascade to see whether debris blockages coincide with high-criticality edges. Do not use this to identify single points of failure or redundancy gaps - that needs an extra-cost-on-removal analysis (remove a candidate edge, re-route, measure the detour), which this tool does not perform.

parameters.name: ROAD_DIRECTION_FIELD
parameters.label: Road direction field (optional: both / ft / bt)

network_emergency_accessibility.help_summary:
Network Emergency Accessibility

Network-distance travel time to the nearest shelter, built on Dijkstra's (1959) shortest-path algorithm - the foundation underneath essentially every network-accessibility GIS tool. Road vertices are snapped into a graph at SNAP_TOLERANCE following the node-snapping approach of Cardinal et al. (2011); a single multi-source Dijkstra traversal seeded from every destination at once replaces one traversal per origin, cutting runtime from O(origins x edges log vertices) to O(edges log vertices).

time_min = net_dist_m / (1000 x SPEED_KMH) x 60, using ONE constant speed for every segment - a highway and a footpath are traversed identically unless you post-process. The default 4.5 km/h is unobstructed walking speed with no stairs, slope, or mobility constraint. A road layer with near-miss endpoints (a common digitising artefact) silently produces a disconnected subgraph rather than an error.

How to read the results - qa_flag = large_snap_distance: the origin sits far from any road vertex - check the road layer for gaps or increase SNAP_TOLERANCE. A high fraction of these across your dataset means the road layer needs re-noding, not a parameter tweak. - qa_flag = not_connected (net_dist_m = -1): the road subgraph containing this origin has no path to any destination - a genuine network-disconnection problem, not a distance problem. - access_cls buckets time_min against TARGET_MINUTES/CRITICAL_MINUTES: Covered / Watch / Underserved / Critical / Unreachable.

Using the results: feed underserved and unreachable origins into Optimal Shelter Siting to find candidate sites that close the gap. This is the network-realistic sibling to the Euclidean Emergency Accessibility and Shelter Coverage tool - use it wherever real street topology matters. It has no capacity or congestion awareness; for that, use Evacuation Time Simulation.

optimal_shelter_siting.help_summary:
Optimal Shelter Siting

Greedy Maximal Covering Location Problem (MCLP, Church & ReVelle, 1974) - the practically-answerable reformulation of Toregas et al.'s (1971) Location Set Covering Problem (minimum facilities to cover ALL demand, often infeasible under a real budget): given a FIXED K, which K candidate sites maximise covered population within MAX_DISTANCE? At each step the greedy algorithm picks the candidate that adds the most still-uncovered demand. Coverage is submodular (diminishing returns per added site, visible directly in the per-step log), so Cornuejols, Fisher & Nemhauser (1977) proved greedy reaches at least (1 - 1/e) is approx 0.63 of the true optimum - and in practice routinely >95% (Daskin, 2013).

Coverage is a hard binary cutoff at MAX_DISTANCE (a unit at 499 m counts fully, 501 m counts zero) using EUCLIDEAN distance - a straight line across a river counts as covered even with no bridge. An optional EXISTING layer pre-covers demand before the greedy loop runs, so the K new picks fill the real remaining gap rather than re-covering what's already served.

How to read the results - oss_selected / oss_rank: which candidates were picked, and in what order. - oss_pop_added: the marginal population each pick added - watch this shrink step over step (diminishing returns) in the processing log; a sharp drop after site 2-3 tells you where the K budget stops paying for itself. - oss_pop_total_cum: running total, compare to the log's overall coverage %.

Using the results: for anywhere real routing barriers matter, pre-route demand through Network Emergency Accessibility first and use the resulting network distance as a coverage-eligibility field instead of raw Euclidean distance. This tool only ADDS sites - it never proposes relocating or removing an existing one. The "top 10 uncovered demand units" log entry identifies populations that may need a mobile response rather than a fixed shelter.

parameters.name: DEMAND
parameters.label: Demand units (points or polygons) with population field

parameters.name: EXISTING
parameters.label: Existing shelters (optional — their coverage is subtracted before greedy)

pareto_optimal_selector.help_summary:
Pareto-Optimal Intervention Selector

Identifies the Pareto frontier of a (cost, benefit) trade-off via non-dominated sorting (NSGA-II style, Deb et al., 2002) - the set of interventions where no other is BOTH cheaper AND more beneficial. Named after Vilfredo Pareto, this is the cornerstone of multi-objective optimisation: rank-1 features are optimal under ANY linear cost-benefit weighting, a stronger guarantee than a single B/C ratio can offer. Pair with the Cost-Benefit Analyzer (uses its cb_cost / cb_benefit outputs) or feed any two numeric trade-off fields.

Per-feature outputs:

  • pareto_rank — 1 = first frontier (best), 2 = second skin after removing the first, etc.
  • pareto_dominated — count of other features that strictly dominate this one.
  • pareto_dominates — count of other features this one strictly dominates.

Only two objectives are considered - real decisions often have more dimensions (equity, co-benefits, political feasibility) this tool cannot represent; treat the frontier as a shortlist for further judgement. Domination is strict and binary, so a feature 0.1% worse on cost but identical on benefit still counts as dominated.

Budget-bounded use: when funds cover only N interventions, picking everything with pareto_rank == 1 guarantees no objectively better alternative exists. Do not use this as the sole selection criterion when non-cost/benefit factors are decisive - it answers which options are efficient, not which should be funded.

parameters.name: INPUT
parameters.label: Layer with cost and benefit fields

pluvial_flood_susceptibility.group: 3 - Flood & Coastal: Pluvial and SLR Susceptibility
pluvial_flood_susceptibility.help_summary:
Pluvial Flood Susceptibility

Topographic screening model in the tradition of Beven & Kirkby's (1979) TOPMODEL wetness-index logic: low, flat, poorly-drained-toward positions pond; high, steep, well-drained-away positions shed water. Rather than a full catchment-contributing-area computation, this tool uses two lightweight DEM proxies a planner can compute in seconds - relative elevation within the study envelope, and local relief within a fixed radius - combined with drainage-line proximity into a 0-100 flood_score, the same "cheap multi-criteria overlay" family validated by Tehrany et al. (2014) for rapid municipal flood-susceptibility mapping.

NEIGHBORHOOD sets the radius for the local-relief (flatness) sample - four cardinal points, not a full slope raster. Without a DRAINAGE layer the drainage term defaults to a neutral 50 rather than failing. DEM sampling is clamped a half-pixel inside the raster extent so cells on the study-area boundary never read outside the DEM. Buildings and roads intersecting cells at or above EXPOSURE_THRESHOLD (default 55) are written to the two exposed-asset outputs.

How to read the results - flood_score >= 75: lowest quartile of the local elevation range, minimal relief, near a drainage line - classic floodplain floor. - flood_score 55-74: transitional slopes near drainage corridors. - flood_score < 35: ridge-top or hillslope cells far from water. - drain_dist = -1 means no DRAINAGE layer was supplied for that run; the drainage component of the score is neutral, not zero.

Using the results: cross-reference exposed buildings with Social Vulnerability Index to find high-exposure + high-vulnerability neighbourhoods, and feed exposed roads into Network Criticality to check whether key evacuation routes sit in flood-prone cells. This is not a hydrodynamic model - it has no rainfall intensity, infiltration, or storm-drain capacity term. Use it for spatial prioritisation and to decide which sub-catchments deserve a real 2D hydrodynamic study; do not use it for regulatory floodplain delineation, insurance rate mapping, or design-storm analysis.

population_weighted_exposure.help_summary:
Population-Weighted Exposure

Translates a 0-100 hazard score into a human-impact estimate, the standard bridge from physical hazard to human impact in disaster-risk literature (UNDRR, 2019) - a hazard score alone says nothing about how many people are affected, which is usually the number that drives budgetary attention. Population is taken either from a field on the scored layer or from a separate point/polygon layer summed inside each unit.

pop_exposed = score/100 x pop_total assumes risk scales linearly with score - a transparent, defensible screening approximation, not a validated dose-response curve for any specific hazard. Population is a snapshot with no diurnal/seasonal variation (daytime workplace vs. nighttime residential population can differ substantially).

Per-unit outputs:

  • pop_total — population in this unit.
  • pop_exposed — score/100 × pop_total.
  • exposure_intensity — Very High / High / Moderate / Low based on the score.
  • exposure_class — same as intensity (kept for symbology naming compatibility).

Study-area summary is printed to the processing log: total population, breakdown by risk class, top 10 units by exposed population.

Using the results: compare pop_exposed rankings against raw score rankings - a moderate-hazard, high-population unit can outrank a high-hazard, low-population one on exposure, a finding this module exists to surface. Where the hazard-to-harm relationship is known to be strongly non-linear (e.g. flood depth-damage curves, typically convex), this linear model understates the difference - use a hazard-specific dose-response function instead.

parameters.name: POP_FIELD
parameters.label: Population field on the scored layer (option A)

parameters.name: POP_LAYER_FIELD
parameters.label: Population field on the population layer (used with option B)

recommended_actions_report.help_summary:
Recommended Actions Report

Reads a scored layer with optional class and dominant-hazard fields, then produces a Markdown report that:

  • summarises score distribution per class,
  • lists the top N highest-scored units,
  • pulls a curated intervention list per detected hazard family from a built-in catalogue.

Catalogue currently covers heat, flood, seismic, social, air, drought and emergency-access. Unknown hazards fall back to a generic checklist.

Hazard-family detection is a transparent, auditable case-insensitive substring match against the dominant-hazard field (e.g. any value containing "flood" maps to the flood catalogue) - not a fuzzy classifier. A field using unexpected terminology (e.g. "inundation" instead of "flood") will not match and falls back to generic. Only ONE dominant hazard per unit drives the checklist, even for units facing several comparably severe hazards.

The catalogue is fixed and identical for every project - it has no awareness of local context, budget, or regulatory environment; every item ("structural retrofit programme", "bioswales along low-lying corridors") is a generic category needing local design and feasibility work, not a costed proposal.

Using the results: if every unit falls back to the generic checklist, check the dominant-hazard field's actual text values against the catalogue keys (heat, flood, seism, social, air, drought, emergency) - a terminology mismatch is the most common cause. Use the checklists to facilitate a stakeholder workshop discussion, not as a ranked or prioritised recommendation.

recovery_capacity_index.help_summary:
Recovery Capacity Index

Measures the OPPOSITE side of resilience: how well a unit can bounce back after a shock, operationalising the "adaptive capacity" dimension of the IPCC AR5 vulnerability framework. Composite of four offline-derivable proxies:

  1. Diversity - Hirschman-Herfindahl Index (borrowed from industrial-organisation economics, where it measures market concentration) applied to land-use shares following Cervero & Kockelman's (1997) "3Ds" framework: many small, evenly-sized land uses signal a healthier local mix than one dominant use.
  2. Redundancy - road-access count, scaled, following the "multiple paths" principle from network resilience theory: a location reachable by several routes recovers service faster after any one route is disrupted.
  3. Green coverage (0-1 or 0-100).
  4. Social cohesion proxy (0-100, e.g. ownership rate or stable-population fraction) - both drawn from Cutter, Ash & Emrich's (2014) validated recovery-capacity indicators.

All four sub-scores are optional and independently excludable - check rc_data_gap before treating a partially-scored unit as comparable to a fully-scored one. REDUNDANCY_SCALE (default 25.0) is a saturation constant, not a fitted parameter: a location with 25+ road-access points scores the maximum 100 regardless of whether it has 25 or 250 - tune it to your study area's actual access-count range. The four sub-scores are treated as independently additive; the model represents no interaction between them (e.g. diverse land uses matter less if nobody can reach them).

Using the results: pair with Adaptation Priority Synthesis or Multi-Hazard Composite to find units that are high-risk AND low-recovery via Risk-Recovery Priority Matrix - the sharpest intervention targets. This uses offline-derivable proxies specifically because they need no survey data; it is not a substitute for a full community-resilience assessment (economic/institutional/social capital surveys) where the stakes justify collecting primary data.

resilience_pdf_atlas.help_summary:
Resilience PDF Atlas

Builds a multi-page atlas (cover + overview + per-class map pages) from a scored resilience layer, automating the standard cartographic "map book" convention: a cover establishing context, an overview orienting the reader, then successive detail pages each isolating one risk class so a reader focuses on one story at a time. Choose a map-book preset (A3 standard, A4 compact, or A3 high-DPI studio). QGIS-native via QgsLayout - every page stays a first-class, editable print layout you can open in the Layout Manager afterward.

Pair with any algorithm in this suite that produces a 0-100 score (Adaptation Priority, Multi-Hazard Composite, Recovery Capacity, Equity-Adjusted Priority, Climate Projection Overlay). The optional class field is used to drive separate pages - use a coarse classification (this suite's standard 4-5 class convention), not a raw continuous score, or the page count can become unwieldy.

Using the results: the 300 dpi Studio preset produces much larger files and longer render times - reserve it for final print production, not quick iterative review. For a fast on-screen check instead of a print deliverable, use Resilience Score HTML Report or Resilience Studio Brief.

resilience_scenario_comparison.help_summary:
Scenario Comparison / Delta Map

Compares two 0-100 score fields on the same layer - baseline vs. proposed intervention, or two alternative planning scenarios - a core methodology in sustainability assessment (Swart et al., 2004; Xiang & Clarke, 2003), following the "comparative statics" tradition of subtracting two spatial fields and mapping the residual. The default 5-point threshold avoids Openshaw & Taylor's (1979) "small change problem": without a threshold every unit shows some delta, most of it noise.

The output adds baseline, scenario, delta, absolute delta, percent change and an improved/stable/worsened class plus an action hint. Lower scores are assumed to be better (this suite's 0-100 scores are always "higher = worse" risk scores). A negative delta therefore means improvement.

How to read the results - change_cls = Improved with a large negative delta: a success-story unit to document and replicate. - change_cls = Worsened: review the scenario parameters - this may be a realistic future-worsening (e.g. climate projection) or a modelling error. - Use percent change for ranking, absolute delta for mapping.

Using the results: this is a same-moment (cross-sectional) comparison of two alternatives, not a longitudinal one - use Resilience Time-Series Tracker for comparing across real time instead. Feed the output into Bivariate Choropleth Symbology with baseline and delta as axes to show "where was it high AND got worse".

parameters.name: INPUT
parameters.label: Planning units with baseline and scenario fields

resilience_score_html_report.help_summary:
Resilience Score HTML Report

Exports a compact, self-contained HTML summary from any polygon or point layer with a 0-100 score field: summary cards (feature count, average, range, high-priority count), a class-distribution table, and a top-drivers table. Front-loads the headline numbers before any table, following standard technical-communication practice (Tufte, 1983) - a reader gets the essentials in the first few seconds.

This is a mirror of the source layer's current field values, not an independent analysis - it re-runs no upstream algorithm, so any upstream error shows up here unchanged, and the file goes stale if the source layer is later edited. Driver/notes text is split on commas and semicolons; a different separator won't tally correctly. The high-priority threshold (>=55) is hard-coded to this suite's standard risk-class convention.

Using the results: a large "missing score values" count is itself a data-quality finding, not just a footnote. Use this for a quick, shareable, no-QGIS-required summary; where narrative prose is needed instead of cards and tables, use Resilience Studio Brief, which generates full sections around the same underlying statistics.

resilience_studio_brief_markdown.help_summary:
Resilience Studio Brief

Creates a Markdown brief from a scored resilience layer, one step up the communication ladder from Resilience Score HTML Report: the same underlying statistics, rendered as narrative prose following the standard structure of a planning-studio memo or policy brief - context, executive summary, evidence, suggested next steps, caveats.

The executive-summary paragraph and suggested-actions list are generated from simple conditional rules on the same average/count statistics (e.g. "if average score >= 55, prioritise near-term design"), not from any additional analysis - a template to edit, not an automated recommendation engine. A standing Limitations section appears on every run by design, so the brief can never be mistaken for a finished, caveat-free document.

It summarizes key score metrics, class distribution, dominant drivers, limitations, and recommended next actions.

Using the results: edit the Study Context paragraph first - the default placeholder is generic and should be replaced with the real study area, timeframe and purpose before the brief leaves the studio. Treat every generated sentence as a first draft a domain expert should verify and very likely rewrite before it reaches an external audience.

parameters.name: STUDY_CONTEXT
parameters.label: Study context
parameters.default: Planning-support screening based on QGIS layers and PlanX Urban Resilience outputs.

resilience_time_series.help_summary:
Resilience Time-Series Tracker

Joins two snapshots of the same scored layer on a stable unit ID and emits per-unit delta, percent change and trend - a two-period panel design, the simplest longitudinal design that can detect direction of change but not acceleration (Cutter & Finch, 2008; Preston et al., 2011 situate this in the climate-adaptation monitoring literature). Trend uses a +/-1 point deadband around zero to suppress rounding/noise from being reported as a real change.

Percent change normalises delta by the baseline (a +10 delta from baseline 20 is +50%, the same +10 from baseline 80 is only +12.5%) - use it for ranking, use the raw delta for mapping on the interpretable 0-100 scale. The optional target-gap field measures distance to a policy target, in the spirit of Sendai Framework monitoring (UNDRR, 2019).

Use cases: monitor a strategy against a 5-year horizon, evaluate a single neighbourhood pre/post-intervention. Geometry is taken from the later snapshot.

How to read the results - ts_trend = No match: the unit ID in the later layer wasn't found in the earlier layer - check for boundary changes or ID-scheme mismatch before assuming the unit simply wasn't scored. - ts_target_gap > 0 AND ts_trend = Worsened: moving away from the policy target, the most concerning trajectory.

Using the results: feed ts_later_score and ts_delta into Risk Trend Hot-Spot for the fused temporal x spatial label. This is for two genuinely time-separated snapshots - for comparing two scenarios at the SAME point in time (baseline vs. proposed), use Scenario Comparison / Delta Map instead.

parameters.name: TARGET_VALUE
parameters.label: Target value (optional, e.g. 30 = aim for risk <= 30)

risk_3d_volume_export.display_name: 3D Risk Volume Export (GeoJSON for PlanX 3D City)
risk_3d_volume_export.help_summary:
3D Risk Volume Export

Turns a 0-100 scored polygon layer into a GeoJSON file with extrusion_height and color_hex attributes so it drops straight into the PlanX 3D City viewer (or Three.js / deck.gl / Cesium) without manual styling - exploiting the human visual system's sensitivity to height variation (Ware, 2012) so equal risk differences read as equal vertical displacement. Colour is deliberately redundant with height (two channels for one variable), improving interpretability for viewers who may not perceive height accurately due to perspective, occlusion, or colour vision deficiency.

The tallest, most saturated blocks in the resulting 3D view are the worst hot spots — a single picture worth a thousand choropleth slides.

GeoJSON is written in EPSG:4326 for web-map compatibility; the in-QGIS vector output keeps the source CRS. MAX_HEIGHT is a display-tuning parameter with no inherent physical meaning - unless BASE_HEIGHT_FIELD carries real building heights and is used additively, extrusion is purely visual, not an actual 3D building model.

Using the results: 3D perspective introduces occlusion (tall extrusions can hide shorter ones) and makes precise value comparison harder than a flat map - keep this alongside the 2D choropleth in a report, not as a replacement for it.

parameters.name: BASE_HEIGHT_FIELD
parameters.label: Optional base height field (metres, added to extrusion)

risk_recovery_priority_matrix.help_summary:
Risk-Recovery Priority Matrix

Combines a hazard or adaptation priority score (0-100) with a recovery capacity score (0-100) into a bivariate risk matrix - the standard ISO 31000 decision-support pattern where a two-axis grid replaces a single number specifically so a decision-maker can see WHY a unit is high-priority, not just THAT it is. The multiplicative form follows the "risk = hazard x vulnerability / coping capacity" convention of the UNDRR risk-assessment framework - structurally the same amplifier pattern as Equity-Adjusted Priority, applied to recovery capacity instead of social vulnerability (the two tools can be chained in either order).

priority = hazard * (1 + w * (100 - recovery) / 100)

The two input scores are assumed independent - in reality well-resourced areas often also have lower physical exposure, which this multiplicative form does not detect or correct for. Recovery capacity is a single scalar (typically rc_score from Recovery Capacity Index), so any nuance about which recovery dimension is weakest is lost by the time it reaches this tool.

Using the results: use the matrix to triage a long list of planning units into four quadrants - Act now (high hazard/low recovery), Prepare (high/high), Support recovery (low/low), Monitor (low hazard/high recovery). Check for correlation between your hazard and recovery fields first - a spuriously high priority can result from two correlated inputs moving together rather than genuinely compounding risk.

risk_trend_hotspot.help_summary:
Risk Trend Hot-Spot

Fuses temporal trend (Δ score between two snapshots) with spatial clustering (Getis-Ord Gi* on the later snapshot) into a single label per unit - the suite's early-warning tool, answering "where is risk both clustered AND getting worse right now." A two-stage design: first compute hot-spot significance on the later snapshot, then annotate with the trend - simpler than a full space-time scan statistic (Kulldorff, 1997) while preserving the key operational insight.

  • Rising / Stable / Cooling hot spot — clustered high values, trajectory tag.
  • Rising / Stable / Cooling cold spot — clustered low values, trajectory tag.
  • Hot / Cold, no cluster — value extreme but not significantly clustered.
  • Not significant.

The significance test is purely spatial and cross-sectional - it does not test whether the CHANGE is clustered, only the current level. Only two time points are used, so this cannot distinguish a genuinely accelerating trend from a single noisy jump; 3+ snapshots would be needed to fit an actual trend line.

Pair with the Resilience Time-Series Tracker output: ts_later_score as the later score and ts_delta as the delta.

Using the results: "Rising hot spot" is the strongest early-warning signal - a statistically significant high-value cluster with an increasing score, the immediate-intervention priority. Check the delta tolerance against the underlying score's known measurement noise before trusting a Rising/Cooling label at face value, especially across closely-spaced snapshots.

parameters.name: INPUT
parameters.label: Layer with later-score and delta fields

parameters.name: DELTA_TOL
parameters.label: Delta tolerance (units below which the trend is 'stable')

scenario_planning_template.help_summary:
Scenario Planning Template

Creates an editable baseline/proposed worksheet from any planning unit or risk layer, following the participatory scenario-planning tradition in land-use and climate-adaptation studies (Patel et al., 2007; Kok et al., 2006): rather than prescribing intervention magnitudes, it gives the planner a starting hypothesis to edit with local knowledge of cost, feasibility and context.

scen_score = base_score x (1 - reduction/100) applies the expected reduction UNIFORMLY as a deliberately naive starting point - every unit is assumed to respond identically, which is almost never true. The tool performs no engineering or spatial validation of the values you enter; edit_status always starts as "draft" as a workflow marker, not a data-quality signal.

Use the output as a clean worksheet before running Scenario Comparison / Delta Map. Lower scores are assumed to be better.

Using the results: (1) filter by edit_status = 'draft' to find units needing review, (2) edit scen_score manually where the uniform reduction is unrealistic, (3) document the reasoning in notes, (4) mark edit_status "reviewed" when done. Ground EXPECTED_REDUCTION in the relevant hazard tool's own literature (e.g. Bowler et al., 2010, for green-cooling magnitude) rather than guessing a number.

parameters.name: DEFAULT_BASE_SCORE
parameters.label: Default baseline score if field is empty

scenario_sensitivity.help_summary:
Scenario Sensitivity Analysis

Stress-tests composite scores by varying component weights with Latin Hypercube Sampling (McKay, Beckman & Conover, 1979) - a stratified Monte Carlo design that explores the full weight space more efficiently than brute-force random sampling. Weight sensitivity is widely recognised as the primary source of rank uncertainty in multi-criteria decision analysis (Saltelli et al., 2004): every composite tool in this suite asks for weights that are policy judgements, not measured constants, and this tool answers "how much does the ranking actually depend on getting those judgements exactly right?"

Each weight is perturbed independently within +/-PERTURB of its nominal value, then renormalised to sum to 1 per sample - weights are NOT modelled as correlated with each other, a simplification of the true weight-elicitation problem. Units with high stability keep a similar composite score regardless of reasonable weight choices; low stability units are sensitive to how hazards are weighted. Stability reflects only the unit's OWN score variance, not whether its RANK relative to other units is stable - two high-stability units can still swap relative order under perturbation.

Outputs: baseline composite (nominal weights), mean, std, p05/p95, range, and a 0-100 stability score.

Using the results: ss_stability < 50 means changing weights by +/-50% shifts the score by more than 12.5 points on average - flag these units as "rank uncertain, review qualitatively" rather than trusting the composite blindly. This tool tells you HOW MUCH the weight choice matters, not what the weights SHOULD be - it is not a substitute for actually engaging stakeholders on the weight choice itself.

seismic_cascade_accessibility.help_summary:
Seismic Cascade — Debris → Network Degradation

Cross-domain cascading-hazard analysis, following the perturb-and-measure methodology formalised in NIST's (2015) Community Resilience Planning Guide: take a baseline network, perturb it with physical damage, measure the resulting service gap. Here the "damage" is the debris-polygon output from Seismic Debris Monte Carlo - this tool pipes it into the road network, drops every edge the debris intersects, builds pre- and post-hazard graphs, and runs multi-source Dijkstra from all destinations on each. The two tools are designed to be run back-to-back, one producing exactly what the other consumes.

Debris blockage is binary - a segment is fully passable or fully blocked, with no partial-capacity reduction for a segment merely narrowed on one side. There is no repair/clearance timeline: the "post" graph is the worst moment immediately after the event, not the gradual reopening that follows. Only debris-driven blockage is modelled - a road segment with genuine pavement or bridge damage but no adjacent building debris is invisible to this tool.

How to read the results - cas_status = Newly cut off: reachable before the quake, isolated after - the intervention-priority class. - cas_status = Worse: still reachable but via a >=1% longer detour (cas_delta_dist > 0). - cas_status = Always cut off: never reachable, pre or post - a pre-existing gap the quake did not create. - Origins and destinations snap to the pre- and post-graphs independently, so a large delta near a blocked segment is worth a map spot-check, not just a table read.

Using the results: run this across several Mw values (6.5, 7.0, 7.5 ...) and compare the Newly-cut-off counts printed to the log to find the magnitude at which the network fails catastrophically rather than gradually. This is not a structural assessment of the road itself - it never asks whether the pavement or a bridge was damaged by shaking, only whether adjacent-building debris blocks it.

seismic_debris_monte_carlo.display_name: Post-Earthquake Collapse, Debris & Evacuation Network (Monte Carlo)
seismic_debris_monte_carlo.help_summary:
Methodology & Theoretical Framework

This module is a stochastic spatial decision-support engine that models structural vulnerability and urban mobility loss for a given earthquake scenario. Base collapse probability is looked up from four construction-era bands modelled on FEMA's HAZUS-MH (2003) fragility framework (pre-1985 0.85, 1985-2000 0.60, 2001-2018 0.25, post-2018 0.05), then scaled exponentially by moment magnitude: mag_factor = exp(0.8 x (Mw - 7.0)). A Monte Carlo simulation draws one Bernoulli collapse outcome per building from that probability, producing a dynamic risk envelope that differs slightly on every run unless the seed is fixed. Debris geometry for a collapsed building follows Goretti & Sarli's (2006) empirically calibrated spread ratio (radius = building height x spread coefficient k); the void/solid volume ratio used to convert footprint area into debris volume follows FEMA P-58 (2018) guidance by construction material. A seed parameter is exposed so a given scenario can be reproduced exactly, or re-rolled by changing the seed to sample a different stochastic realisation of the same magnitude.

Input Parameter Guide

Parameter Description & Recommended Values
Moment Magnitude (Mw) Earthquake energy. Has an exponential effect on the fragility function (e.g. 7.0 - 7.6).
Debris Spread Coefficient (k) Fraction of a collapsed building's height thrown horizontally onto adjacent roads (Goretti & Sarli, 2006). Typically 0.30 to 0.50.
Void/Solid Volume Ratio Fraction of the gross building volume that becomes actual debris (concrete/brick). Per FEMA guidance:
• Steel/Glass: 0.10 - 0.20
• Reinforced concrete (RC): 0.25 - 0.35
• Unreinforced masonry: 0.35 - 0.45
Random Seed Fixes the Monte Carlo draw so results are reproducible run-to-run; change it to sample a different stochastic realization of the same scenario.

Output Schema

  • [01_Static] Net Logistics Network Topology: Cadastral road/void fabric with building footprints subtracted.
  • [02_Static] Morphological Conflict: Static form index modelling encroachments onto parcel boundaries as negative vectors.
  • [03_Dynamic] Stochastic Risk & Volume Index: Point layer with collapse probability, estimated debris volume (m3), and severity class per building.
  • [04_Dynamic] Macro-Debris Spread Envelope: Dissolved debris polygon covering all collapsed buildings.
  • [05_Dynamic] Critical Network Blockage Areas: Cumulative debris mass that falls specifically on the road network.
  • [06_Dynamic] Post-Disaster Active Evacuation Corridors: Remaining accessible routes for search-and-rescue logistics.

How to Read the Results

  • collapse_prob sorts your retrofit-priority list: buildings above 0.80 under a Mw > 7.0 scenario are pre-code construction and the first candidates for structural assessment.
  • collapsed (0/1) is this run's Monte Carlo outcome, not a certainty - re-run with a different seed to see how sensitive the network-blockage picture is to the specific draw.
  • debris_vol_m3 and blocked_area_m2 scale with building height and footprint - a single tall building can outweigh several low ones in total road-blockage impact.
  • [06] Evacuation Corridors is the headline output for response planning: what survives once [05]'s blockages are subtracted from the network.

Using the Results

Compare Mw 6.5 against Mw 7.5 runs (same seed) to see the exponential, non-linear jump in road loss between a moderate and a major event - this is usually more informative for planning than a single "design" magnitude. Feed [04] Macro-Debris Envelope into Seismic Cascade: Debris -> Network Degradation for the full pre- vs. post-quake accessibility comparison, and [03] Structural Damage Index into Population-Weighted Exposure to translate collapse probabilities into estimated human impact. This is a planning-screening tool, not an engineering-grade structural assessment - do not use individual collapse_prob values to make retrofit funding decisions without a site inspection.
