social_vulnerability_index.help_summary:
Social Vulnerability Index

Composite 0-100 vulnerability score in the Cutter, Boruff & Shirley (2003) Social Vulnerability Index (SoVI) tradition, which established that vulnerability to hazards is a property of people and places independent of any one hazard. Up to five indicators - elderly, children, disability, low-income and population density - are each min-max normalised 0-100 within the supplied layer, then combined by weighted mean. Default weights (elderly 0.25, low-income 0.25, disability 0.20, children 0.15, density 0.15) track the relative importance Cutter & Finch (2008) reported for these dimensions; unlike the original SoVI's principal-components analysis, every step here is a transparent, auditable weighted sum - easier to explain to a planning board, at the cost of not correcting for correlation between indicators the way factor analysis does.

All indicators are treated as risk-increasing; to represent a protective factor (e.g. high home-ownership, strong social cohesion), invert its sign in a Field Calculator expression before running this tool. Any field left blank is skipped and listed in data_flags rather than blocking the run - a partial score is still computed from whatever indicators are present. Keep the layer in a metric CRS when a population field is supplied, since density = population / polygon area in hectares.

How to read the results - svi_score >= 75: the most vulnerable areas in this layer - multiple overlapping indicators, and the equity-priority targets. - svi_score 55-74: elevated vulnerability, typically one dominant factor. - data_flags: "ok" means every indicator carrying non-zero weight had data; otherwise it lists which ones were missing, so a partial score is never mistaken for a complete one. - Because normalisation is relative to this layer's own value range, scores are only comparable within one run - re-running on a different extent changes every score, and scores from two different runs should not be compared directly.

Using the results: feed svi_score into Equity-Adjusted Adaptation Priority to raise the priority of high-hazard + high-vulnerability units, or into Risk-Recovery Priority Matrix alongside a recovery-capacity score to find where the two diverge most. This is a planning-support index for relative prioritisation, not a substitute for the full peer-reviewed SoVI or CDC/ATSDR SVI computation, and not suitable for cross-city comparison without re-basing both layers to a common reference range.

synthetic_resilience_demo_dataset.help_summary:
Synthetic Resilience Demo Dataset

Generates a complete artificial city block in one run - nine layers (study area, buildings, roads, impervious surfaces, green infrastructure, water, shelters, social units, sensitive receptors) built from a fixed cellular template, not a statistical or agent-based city generator. This is a test fixture in the software-testing sense (Fisher & Tate, 2006): the layout is deterministic, so the same SCALE value always produces byte-identical geometry across runs and machines.

Output CRS is fixed to EPSG:3857 (metric, projected). SCALE (default 1.0, range 0.25-5.0) scales the whole layout uniformly in metres - it does not add more features, only stretches the same relative geometry. Buildings carry floor_count / land_use / year / population; roads carry class / capacity_ph / direction; social units carry population / elderly / children / disability / low_income - the exact field names the hazard and synthesis modules in this suite expect, so every other tool accepts these layers with no preparation.

How to read the results - Nine layers land in the project after one run; none need further editing before feeding them into another tool. - Attribute values (floor counts, population figures, construction years) are hand-picked plausible numbers, not sampled from any census or building-stock survey - read nothing into their specific magnitudes. - Geometry is fixed relative to SCALE, so two runs at the same SCALE are identical; this is what makes the dataset a reliable regression fixture.

Using the results: run this first on a new install, or after any code change, to confirm every one of the other 42 algorithms accepts its inputs without error; use it for classroom demonstrations where every student needs an identical starting dataset. Do not use it for any published or decision-supporting analysis, and do not use it to test edge cases the fixed template does not contain (disconnected networks, multipart geometries, missing CRS) - build a dedicated fixture for those instead.

urban_heat_comfort_risk.help_summary:
Urban Heat Comfort Risk

Screening model for urban heat exposure, built on Oke's (1982) energy-balance account of the urban heat island: reduced sky-view, low-albedo/impervious materials and building mass all raise surface heat storage, while green space and water provide measurable local cooling (Bowler et al., 2010 meta-analysis; effective range roughly 200-400 m). Each grid cell gets a 0-100 heat_score from four additive, user-weighted components: impervious share, building density, a green deficit / cooling-distance term, and optional vulnerable-asset proximity - the same land-cover surrogates used in Stewart & Oke's (2012) Local Climate Zone framework, since real air/surface temperature is rarely available to a planning studio.

CELL_SIZE trades resolution for runtime (smaller cells = more cells to score). COOLING_DISTANCE (default 400 m) is the walking distance within which a park or water body counts as accessible cooling - every qualifying feature counts equally regardless of its size or canopy density. Without an IMPERVIOUS layer, that component reads 0; without GREEN/WATER, the cooling term reads worst-case (100).

How to read the results - heat_score >= 75 (Very High): dense building clusters, almost no green space, far from water - the classic UHI core. - heat_score 55-74 (High): residential districts with moderate tree cover but high impervious share. - heat_score < 35 (Low): park-adjacent or water-adjacent cells. - Priority cooling zones (heat_score >= 55) are the intervention shortlist, not a temperature forecast - the score is a relative land-cover composite, not a measured or simulated air temperature.

Using the results: cross-reference priority cooling zones with Population-Weighted Exposure to find cells where high heat risk coincides with high population density, and feed them into Cost-Benefit Analyzer to rank tree-planting or reflective-pavement interventions. Do not use heat_score to predict actual temperature or a heat-index value - that needs a real microclimate simulation or land-surface-temperature retrieval.

vulnerability_surface_idw.help_summary:
Vulnerability Surface (IDW)

Interpolates sparse point measurements (sensor readings, survey scores, social-cohesion samples) into a continuous surface as polygon grid cells using inverse-distance weighting (Shepard, 1968) - the earliest general-purpose deterministic spatial interpolator, needing no variogram fitting or distributional assumptions, only a distance function and a power parameter. Power p=1 gives gentle gradients; p=4 gives sharp peaks that decay quickly around each sample.

IDW is an exact interpolator (the estimate at a sample point equals the observed value exactly) with no built-in uncertainty estimate, unlike kriging. It assumes spatial dependence decays smoothly and isotropically - it cannot represent directional trends or genuine discontinuities across a boundary.

Per-cell outputs:

  • vs_value — interpolated value.
  • vs_class — Very High / High / Moderate / Low (standard 0-100 thresholds).
  • vs_n_points — number of source points that contributed (after radius / neighbour cap).

Cells outside the study-area polygon are skipped. vs_n_points = 0 marks an extrapolation gap (no source point within radius - reduce power or increase radius); vs_n_points = 1 means the cell's value equals the single nearest point exactly, an exact-interpolation artefact worth increasing the radius to smooth out.

Using the results: use this for a fast, dependency-free surface where an approximate continuous picture beats no picture. Where a rigorous uncertainty estimate matters for the decision, a proper geostatistical method (kriging) is the standard alternative, since IDW has no statistically principled confidence measure.

wui_exposure_screening.group: 7 - Drought & Wildfire: Green and WUI Stress
wui_exposure_screening.help_summary:
Wildfire / Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) Exposure Screening

Screens a study area for Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) wildfire exposure by combining wildland vegetation fuel proximity and cover (Radeloff et al., 2005), structure-to-vegetation interface density within the radiant/ember ignition zone (Cohen, 2000), topographic slope rate-of-spread amplification (Rothermel, 1972), and emergency road egress deficit (Cova, 2005).

For each grid cell, the 0-100 wui_score is the weighted combination of four standardized sub-scores: (1) fuel_score (vegetated cover share in the cell plus inverse distance to the wildland fuel boundary within WUI_BUFFER), (2) inter_score (density of buildings intersecting the WUI fuel buffer), (3) slope_score (finite-difference slope percentage from the optional DEM, scaled linearly across 0-35%% slope; defaults to neutral 50.0 with slope_pct = -1.0 when no DEM is supplied), and (4) egress_score (distance to the nearest evacuation road relative to MAX_EGRESS_DIST).

How to read the results: cells with wui_score >= 60 are exported to the priority WUI intervention layer, and structures inside the radiant/ember buffer of cells scoring >= 55 are written as point features to the exposed interface structures layer. This is a planning-scale exposure screening model and does not simulate wind-driven firebrand transport or fuel moisture physics.
